activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
Christopher refreshed the page for the fourth time that morning, and the price of the Glacier Fox trading card had climbed again, from eighteen dollars to twenty-two. He needed that card. His collection was missing exactly one fox, and a kid at school named Quintin had been reminding him of it all week.

"Tell your dad it's for school," Quintin had said at lunch, which was useless advice, because twenty-two dollars was twenty-two dollars no matter what you called it.

Christopher typed a message to the seller, a collector named Azalea who ran an online marketplace stall with rows of card photos behind an opaque privacy screen so nobody could see her address. He offered fifteen dollars. She replied in two minutes: "Can't. Ten people asked me today. Last month I couldn't sell it at twelve."

He stared at that message for a long time. Last month it was cheaper than he was offering now, and nobody wanted it. Now everybody wanted it and the price shot up. He dragged a notebook over and made two columns, one for what buyers were doing, one for what Azalea had in her stall. Then he called Quintin, because arguing with Quintin always made his thinking sharper.

"Sellers set the price," Quintin said. "It's Azalea's stall. She types the number."

"No way, buyers set it. Ten people asked today. That's why she raised it."

They went back and forth until Azalea herself joined the chat, since she could see the whole thread. "You're both right, sort of," she typed. "There's an old economist, Alfred Marshall. In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics' he compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price."

"Scissors," Christopher said out loud, and Quintin went quiet on the other end, thinking.

"So if I wait," Christopher typed slowly, "and the fox stops being scarce, and people stop asking, the price falls?"

"That's the other blade," Azalea wrote. "I'd rather sell it than hold it forever."

He waited eleven days. He refreshed the page every morning, watching the price sit at twenty-two, then wobble, then drop to nineteen, then to sixteen. On the twelfth day he bought the card for sixteen dollars, and after he clicked confirm he opened his notebook and drew a pair of scissors beside his two columns, then set the notebook under the lamp so the drawing dried flat.

"Buyers and sellers," he told Quintin on the phone. "Both blades."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: An answer like six eighths should be simplified by dividing the top and bottom by their greatest common factor, 2, to get three quarters.
story:
The tutoring centre occupied the back room of a dilapidated old bookstore, where the radiator clanked and the ceiling fan wobbled on its lowest speed. Levi sat at the scratched table with his worksheet, chewing his pencil. He had promised his mother he would pass Friday's retest on fractions, and Ms. Demetriou had agreed to stay late. He wanted the pizza party on Friday more than almost anything, and only students who passed could go.

On the page, three fourths plus three eighths waited for him. He knew enough to change the first fraction so both bottoms matched; he wrote six eighths plus three eighths, then nine eighths, and sat back. Across the table, Aleena slid her marked quiz toward him. "Look at this," she said. "I got it right but there's a note." Her answer read six eighths, and beside it Ms. Demetriou had written "right, but unfinished." Aleena frowned. "How can it be right and unfinished at the same time?"

Levi studied the two fractions on her page, six eighths and the original one fourth plus one half it had come from. He noticed something. Both the top and the bottom were even numbers, which meant two would go into each of them. He tried it quietly on scrap paper: six divided by two was three, and eight divided by two was four. Three quarters. It looked like an answer he'd seen in the back of the book for that exact problem. "I think you have to divide the top and the bottom by two," he said. "Six eighths is really three quarters." Aleena squinted at it, then nodded slowly. "So my answer wasn't wrong, it just wasn't done yet. I'm redoing the whole quiz tonight."

Ms. Demetriou came over and set two more worksheets on the table. "Want to check his idea against the answer key?" Levi found the page and ran his finger down the column. There it was, three quarters, printed neat and small. He grinned and copied his own answer over, crossing out nine eighths and starting again. "Show me the one with the twelfths," Aleena said, pulling her chair closer.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
Daniel stood backstage at the community center with his word list, glaring at the word "bite." Why keep an e that said nothing? He flipped the card over as if the answer might be hiding there. It wasn't, but a faded poster on the wall behind him was, half covered by the trophy case. The building had once belonged to a merchants' guild, the poster said, and its old library had been left in the basement.

He slipped downstairs during the break. Juliet followed him, arms crossed. "You're going to miss your turn," she warned.

"Look," Daniel said, pulling a dusty book from a shelf. It was about the history of English. He turned pages until a chapter heading stopped him cold. "Listen to this. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed. It's called the Great Vowel Shift."

"So people just decided to talk weird?"

"No, it says spellings had already started to become fixed before the sounds changed. The letters stayed put and the sounds moved." He read the line twice. "That's why spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. The words aren't trying to trick me. They're just old."

Juliet leaned over the page, and her frown loosened into something like interest. "So 'bite' used to be said differently, and the spelling is like a fossil."

He had always thought of tricky spellings as a sinister plot against him personally, but the book made them seem almost friendly, like footprints left behind by a word that had wandered off. "Can I confide something?" he said. "I was going to quit. I told my dad I'd fake a stomachache."

"You're not going to now?"

"No," Daniel said, and he meant it.

Back upstairs, the pronouncer gave him "thrice." Daniel pictured the vowel sounds shifting like tectonic plates while the letters stood still, and he understood why the i said its long name. "T-H-R-I-C-E," he said. "Thrice."

The bell rang for correct, and Juliet, who had spent a week saying spelling bees were for robots, was on her feet clapping loudest of all.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: Where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, a flood of local berries raises the supply all at once, which usually pushes their price down.
story:
Eli stood in front of the berry stall at the farmers' market and read the sign twice, because the first time he was sure he had misread it. Strawberries, two dollars a basket. In March, when his mom had bought them for his birthday shortcake, the same baskets had cost four. He tugged Janelle's sleeve. "Look. Is this a mistake?"

Janelle squinted at the sign, then at the farmer, who was busy restacking flats to expose the deepest red berries at the front of the table. "Maybe they're bad ones," she said, picking up a basket anyway. They smelled sweet, like summer itself, warm even in the shade of the canopy. Eli bought two baskets with his own money and carried them through the crowd, turning the puzzle over. Same berries, half the price. Something invisible had changed between March and June, and he wanted to know what.

He tested his first idea right there: maybe the farmer was desperate, going out of business. But the line at the stall was ten people long, and the farmer, who rented the spot and was, according to the banner overhead, the market's longest-standing tenant, looked anything but desperate. So Eli tried the opposite idea. He counted the stalls as they walked. One, two, three more berry farmers, all piled high, all with the same low prices. He stopped so suddenly that a man carrying bread almost walked into him. "It's not one farm," he said. "It's all of them. In March nobody around here has berries ripe outdoors, so there aren't many. Now, in early summer, they all come ripe at once. A whole flood of local berries hits the market together." Janelle nodded slowly. "So the supply goes way up," she said, "and the price comes down."

That night Eli wrote a message to Elody, who had missed the trip because of a soccer tournament. "You won't believe this. Summer strawberries are HALF what they cost in March. I figured out why. Around here the berries ripen outdoors in early summer, and they all arrive at the market at the same time. All those local berries raise the supply at once, and that pushes the price down. In March there's barely any supply, so the price is high. Come with us next Saturday. Bring four dollars and you'll come home with four baskets."

She answered an hour later with a photo of a strawberry the size of her fist and one line: "Deal. But if the price doubles again before Saturday, I'm blaming you."

Eli grinned, set his phone on the desk, and went downstairs to slice berries for cereal, sweet red circles falling one by one into the bowl.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediators sometimes meet with each side privately, and this separate meeting is called a caucus.
story:
Nora had planned to spend Saturday eating dumplings and doing nothing, but her mother had invited Harleen and Charles-Antoine to dinner, and by the time the soup arrived the two of them were not speaking. Nora knew the silence was about the group project, because Harleen's science presentation had gone first, and Charles-Antoine's had gone second, and his was suspiciously similar to hers, right down to the joke about plankton.

"You could just ask them," Nora's mother said, ladling dumplings into bowls.

"They won't talk in front of each other," Nora said. "They'll just do the frozen face thing."

Harleen's frozen face was already in place. Charles-Antoine's was slightly defiant, chin up, as if he had been waiting all evening for someone to accuse him so he could deny it.

Nora thought about it while she ate. When her parents argued about the thermostat, her father never solved anything in the living room. He followed her mother into the kitchen, and they talked in low voices, and when they came out the argument was somehow over. Nora could not see what happened in there, but she had started to notice the pattern: the private talk came first, the peace came second. Maybe that was the formula. Maybe people could not back down with an audience, so you had to catch them without one.

She swallowed her last dumpling and stood up. "Harleen, come help me in the kitchen."

In the kitchen, Harleen stacked two bowls that did not need stacking. "I'm not saying he cheated," she said. "I'm saying his presentation had my exact plankton joke, word for word."

"Okay," said Nora. "That's all I needed." She marched back out, collected Charles-Antoine, and installed him by the sink. He attempted a casual expression, but it could not conceal the fact that he was holding a whisk like a shield.

"I saw Harleen's slideshow when she practiced Tuesday," he said quietly. "In the library. I didn't copy it, I just... remembered it."

"So the plankton joke was hers."

"It was a good joke," he admitted, deflating slightly. "It followed me home."

Nora brought Harleen back in. "You two are going to talk, and I'm going to stand here and eat these fortune cookies and not take a side. The kitchen thing I did, where I meet each of you alone, has a name. My uncle does it at his work. It's called a caucus."

Charles-Antoine frowned. "Sounds like a type of bird."

"It's not a bird. Say sorry about the joke and move on."

Harleen folded her arms, then unfolded them. "Say the plankton joke is mine out loud, in the living room, where my brother can hear it, and we're fine."

Charles-Antoine walked to the doorway and called it out, twice, louder the second time. Then he sat down and reached for a fortune cookie. Nora took the last one before he could.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptian pyramids were built on the west bank of the Nile, the side where the sun sets, which Egyptians linked with death and the afterlife.
story:
Sarah pressed her nose against the bus window as the museum's glass doors came into view. Today was the day her class would present their pyramid projects at the Egyptian exhibition, and she had promised Ms. Rahman she could explain why the pyramids were built and how the Nile shaped Egyptian farming.

"Move over," said Landon, dropping into the seat beside her. He unrolled the huge map of Egypt he'd borrowed from the library. "I made this at two in the morning. My mom was thrilled."

Maxime leaned across the aisle. "Let me see. Whoa, it's huge."

The three of them spread the map flat across their knees. Sarah traced the blue line of the Nile with her finger, the river running like a long ribbon down the desert. Then she stopped. "Wait. Look at the pyramids. Every single one we marked is on the west side of the river. All of them. Why would that be?"

Landon squinted at the map. "That's weird. It's not a coincidence if it's every pyramid."

"It's like a rule," said Maxime. "A hidden rule nobody wrote down."

Sarah remembered the evening her grandmother had shown her old photographs from her own trip to Egypt, standing on a boat at sunset, watching the sun sink into the desert hills while the water turned gold. Sarah had felt a flash of envy then, wishing she could see it herself. "The sun sets in the west," she said slowly. "Egyptians connected the west with death and the afterlife. So they built their pyramids on the west bank of the Nile, the side where the sun sets."

She said it like a guess, but it felt like a key turning. To test it, she flipped through her notebook to the page about the Nile and farming. Every spring the river flooded, leaving dark, wet mud on the fields, and farmers grew their wheat in it. The flood was why farms lined the river in the first place. The river fed them, and the west bank is where they buried their dead.

"It's hypothetical until we check," said Maxime, "but it fits the map perfectly."

At the museum, Ms. Rahman set them up near a wall-sized satellite photo of the Nile. "Sarah, you're first. Show us why the pyramids are where they are."

Sarah's heart drummed. She pointed to the river. "The Nile flooded every year, and that mud made farming possible. That's why everyone lived near it." Then she slid her finger to the western side. "And the pyramids are all on this side, the west bank, where the sun sets, because Egyptians linked the west with death and the afterlife."

A woman from the museum, overhearing, smiled and gave her a thumbs up. Landon grinned and whispered, "Nailed it."

"Best school trip income ever," Maxime joked, holding out his hand for a high five.

Sarah slapped it, still staring at the great river winding through the photograph. "Same time tomorrow?"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
story:
Lucas stood in his uncle's kitchen, staring at the plastic bin his cousin had labeled BEAR LOCKER STUFF. They were leaving for Yosemite in an hour, and Lucas had already packed his bag twice. "Why does the granola go in the bin?" he asked Reese, who lived next door and had invited himself along. Reese shrugged. "Bears, obviously." But Lucas kept turning the idea over. Bears could not read labels. How would a bear know what was inside a tent?

At the campground that evening, the metal locker by their site was already half full, and Lucas studied it like a puzzle. Peanut butter, chips, trash bag. Then he noticed his uncle stashing sunscreen and a tube of toothpaste inside, and the pieces clicked into place. "It's not just food," Lucas said slowly. "It's anything with a smell." His uncle nodded without looking up. "In bear country, parks like Yosemite count anything with a scent as food. Toothpaste, sunscreen, trash, all of it goes in." Lucas tested the idea against everything he could see. Minty toothpaste, coconut sunscreen, even the empty wrapper in his pocket. He added the wrapper to the locker and felt oddly satisfied, like he had spotted an adversary's next move before it happened.

That night, Lucas woke to a scraping sound outside the tent. He lay still, heart hammering. His cousin's voice whispered, "Did you leave anything out?" Lucas ran through the locker in his mind, item by item, and came up neutral, nothing forgotten. Then he remembered Mason, who had joined them at the last minute and set up his own tent, grumbling that the locker was too far.

Lucas crawled out with the flashlight. Mason was standing by his tent holding his toothpaste, frozen, while a dark shape moved between the trees. "Throw it," Lucas hissed. Mason hurled the tube toward the locker, and Lucas banged the door shut just as the shape ambled away into the dark. "Remind me," Mason whispered, "to pack minty things last."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
story:
Theodore set six bean plants in a row along the kitchen windowsill, each one in a yogurt cup with a marker taped to the side. His friend Alina leaned over the counter, poking at the bottles of plant food he had lined up beside the sink.

"Which one are we giving the magic juice?" she asked. She had wanted the blue bottle ever since they bought it, because the label showed a bean plant the size of a small tree.

"All of them," Theodore said. "That's the whole project. We feed them Booster Gro for two weeks and measure how tall they get."

Alina frowned. "My brother won the science fair with a volcano. A volcano, Theodore. If all our plants grow, how do we know Booster Gro did it? Maybe beans just grow fast anyway."

Theodore looked at the cups. The plants were all the same size now, all the same soil, all the same windowsill light. If every single one got the fertilizer, and they all shot up, he'd have no way to know whether the blue stuff deserved the credit or whether the beans would have grown like that anyway. He tried to reassure Alina with the promise that the project was still salvageable. "We keep three plants exactly the same as the other three," he said, pulling three cups to the left end of the counter. "Same soil, same water, same spot. The only difference is those three get Booster Gro and these three get nothing."

"Like a control group," Alina said.

"Ms. Zhou would be so proud she'd cry," Theodore said.

They built a cardboard divider with a flap so the fertilizer plants could be watered with the solution without splashing the others. Alina held up a paper scale she'd made from a cereal box. "Prototype measuring stick," she announced. "Only trivial problems, like it's two centimeters short."

"For you, everything is trivial," Theodore said, and sprinkled the first blue drops on cup number one.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action.
story:
Sawyer counted the chalk marks on the curb where Avi had nearly gotten hit last month, seven in two weeks, all from kids crossing Grosvenor Street to get to school. The city had never painted a crosswalk there, and nobody at school could say why.

"Maybe they just forgot," Brodie said, spinning his skateboard with one foot.

"They didn't forget," Sawyer said. "There's no crosswalk because nobody ever asked for one. Not officially. My mom says city hall doesn't do things because people complain at the bus stop. They do things because somebody files the right paper."

Mr. Yilmaz, who ran the hardware store on the corner and had signed more than his share of city paperwork, leaned on his broom in the doorway. "You want the councillor's attention, you need a petition," he said. "A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking the government to take a specific action."

"A specific action," Sawyer repeated, writing it on his hand. "So not 'make the street safer.' It has to be 'paint a crosswalk at Grosvenor and Elm.'"

"That's the idea," Mr. Yilmaz said, and went back to sweeping.

That afternoon, Sawyer drafted the wording three times. His first version said the crossing was dangerous, which Brodie liked, but Sawyer crossed it out. Complaining wasn't a specific action. The second version asked for "safety improvements," which sounded like a wish list. The third said exactly what they wanted, one sentence, with room below for names and addresses. He photocopied twenty sheets at the library for a dollar.

Saturday, they set up outside Mr. Yilmaz's store. Avi held the clipboard while Brodie explained the near-misses to anyone who slowed down. A tenant from the apartment above the store came down in slippers and signed. Mr. Yilmaz signed. A woman who ran the bakery signed and said her delivery driver had begged for a crosswalk for a year. By four o'clock they had sixty-three signatures, and Sawyer noticed something he hadn't expected: the names clustered in a pattern. Nearly everyone who signed lived or worked within two blocks of the corner.

"That makes sense," he told Avi, spreading the pages on his bedroom floor that night. "The people who cross here every day are the ones who want it changed." He put a star beside the bakery woman, because she had said the delivery driver would sign too, and a driver who couldn't park was almost the equivalent of a pedestrian who couldn't cross. The petition needed people affected by the problem, not just people who felt bad about it.

On Monday, they took the bus to city hall. The clerk at the front counter looked fifteen, which made Sawyer less nervous, and she read every page. "This is good," she said. "You'd be surprised how many people bring me a sheet that says 'fix stuff.'" She stamped it and told him the councillor's office would review it and schedule it for a council meeting. Sawyer asked whether he could speak at the meeting. She said anyone could speak for three minutes, and handed him a green slip to reserve a spot.

He walked out holding the slip like it might blow away. In the plaza in front of city hall, Brodie pointed at the fountain and said, "Three minutes is not very long."

"It's longer than we've ever had before," Sawyer said, folding the slip into quarters and putting it in his back pocket, the safest pocket, the one he always checked twice.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear.
story:
Sadie stood in the wings of the gymnasium with her violin under her chin, watching the chairs fill. In ten minutes the spring concert would begin, and she had never once played on a stage. The folded program in her pocket had her name in it, printed small: Sadie Okafor, violin. She read it four times.

Syeda popped up beside her. "Why does everyone stand around doing nothing until the oboe plays? We just wait for one note. It's weird." She pointed at Markus, who sat third chair in the woodwinds, holding his oboe like it might go off.

Sadie had noticed the same thing at every rehearsal. Mr. Suryanto would raise his hand, the room would go silent, and Markus would play a single A. Then the violins, cellos, and trumpets would all adjust their tuning to that one sound. She had a theory, and during the warm-up she decided to test it. While the brass was tuning, she turned her fine tuner a quarter turn sharp, so her A string no longer matched. When she bowed it against Markus's note, her string beat against his like two wings flapping out of rhythm. She turned the peg back until the wobbling stopped. The note sat still. Her string had nothing steady to match until his sounded first.

Before she could say anything, a seventh grader handed her a note from the piano bench. It was folded into a triangle. "Can't find my A," it said. "Fork in my case. HELP. Markus." Sadie looked over. He was sweating. She wrote back, "Just play your A like always. You always sound the same. That's the whole point," and sent it back by way of Syeda.

The gym lights dimmed. Mr. Suryanto lifted his hand, the audience hushed, and Markus stood, took a breath, and played one clear, penetrating A that reached every corner of the gym. Sixty students turned their pegs toward it. Sadie matched her string to his, set her bow on the string, and waited for the downbeat.

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: Hurdlers try to run over hurdles rather than jump them, staying low so they spend as little time in the air as possible.
story:
Rachel had signed up for the pool club's dry-land track session mostly because Peyton and Rayne had, and now she stood on the grass beside the fence, staring at a row of four low white hurdles. Mr. Bondarenko clapped his hands and said the drill was simple: three steps between each hurdle, all the way down the row.

Peyton went first and flew over every hurdle like it was nothing. Then Rayne went, and Rachel watched him leap high, both feet tucked up, landing hard and scrambling to rebuild his speed. He crossed the finish three full seconds behind Peyton's time. Rachel was next, and she did exactly what Rayne had done, springing as high as she could, and finished even slower.

Between turns she stood at the fence, chewing the strap of her goggles, and studied Peyton. The contradiction bothered her. Peyton was not the fastest sprinter in their grade; Rachel had beaten her in the fifty-meter dash at school. Yet here Peyton was untouchable. There had to be something hidden going on, some cause Rachel could not see from the sidelines, and she meant to find it.

"Can I watch you again?" she asked. "Just your feet."

Peyton ran the row a second time. This time Rachel caught it. Peyton barely left the ground. Her lead leg snapped over the top and her trail leg swung through sideways, low, quick, almost lazy, as if she were running over the hurdles instead of jumping them. Rachel filed that away. Rayne's extravagant leaps looked impressive, but every extra inch in the air was time spent not moving forward.

When her turn came, Rachel sprinted at the first hurdle and simply kept running, attacking it, letting her leg cut across the top. Three steps. Another hurdle, the same thing, low and fast. She crossed the line and looked at the stopwatch in Mr. Bondarenko's hand before he said a word.

"Half a second behind Peyton," he announced. "Down from three."

Rayne jogged over, frowning. "Okay, teach me."

Rachel grinned and pointed at the first hurdle. "Stop jumping. Just run through the top of it."

"Through it?"

"Over it," Rachel said, "but low. Come on, I'll mediate between you and that middle hurdle if I have to."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: During Ramadan, Muslims eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer, then go without food and drink until sunset.
story:
The alarm went off at 3:47 in the morning, and Charlie sat up in her sleeping bag on her aunt's living room floor. The kitchen light was already on. Her cousin Mercedes was at the table in her pajamas, cracking eggs into a pan, and their grandmother was filling a thermos of water.

"Come on," Mercedes said. "It's easier if you eat with everybody."

Charlie had decided to try the fast with her aunt's family for one day, and she had a plan written on a napkin in her pocket. She figured the hard part would be lunchtime, when she could see it and smell it, so her plan was to eat a huge amount now, at suhur, and conquer her hunger before it started. She filled her plate with eggs, toast, yogurt, and a glass of milk, and then a second glass.

"It's called suhur," her grandmother said, setting down the teapot. "The meal before the dawn prayer."

After the prayer, everyone went back to bed. Charlie woke again at ten, and her stomach already felt tight. She drank nothing, because she'd worked out the night before that this was the tricky part: she could survive missing food, but no water until sunset meant she had to pace herself. Her plan had a flaw she hadn't expected. Eating twice as much now didn't stop hunger later; it just made her thirsty earlier.

Mercedes spent the whole day building a prototype of a solar oven out of a pizza box and foil on the back porch. She wanted to bake the sunset bread herself, without the regular oven, and she kept dragging Charlie out to adjust the angles. Around four o'clock, Charlie sat on the porch step and admitted her experiment had gone wrong.

"I ate double," she said. "I thought it would store up."

"Everybody tries that the first time," Mercedes said, not looking up from the foil. "It doesn't work like that."

At sunset they heard the call to prayer from the mosque two streets over, and Mercedes's bread, which had turned out only slightly controversial in color, came off the foil warm and flat. Charlie drank a full glass of water in four swallows.

"Same time tomorrow?" Mercedes asked.

Charlie tore off a piece of bread. "Set the alarm."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
Mr. Rosen had written "Claim vs. Story" on the board and given them twenty minutes to finish their evidence sheets before the bell, and Lucy was stuck at the third question with Reid's binder in front of her.

Reid wouldn't put his hand anywhere near the class fish tank, even though it held four guppies and one extremely temporary crayfish borrowed from another room. "It's not the fish," he kept saying. "It's water. My uncle's coworker got bitten by a shark last summer, and he showed us the scar. I'm not swimming in the lake trip on Friday. That's my claim: lakes are dangerous."

"That's not a claim," Lucy said. "That's one guy's scar." She was already flipping through the chapter Mr. Rosen had left open, half to win the argument and half because the sheet was due in fourteen minutes and she had nothing. The page mentioned two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, who in 1973 described something that made her stop reading and start grinning.

"Reid. Listen. There's a thing called the availability heuristic." He frowned, so she said it slower. "It means people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. Your uncle's story comes to mind super easily because of the scar. So swimming feels more dangerous than it is."

"That's a word, not a test," Reid said, which was annoyingly exactly what the worksheet asked for. Lucy glanced at the clock. Twelve minutes. She grabbed a marker and drew a line down the whiteboard, wrote SHARK on one side and BEE on the other. "Everybody!" she called, and Saad looked up from his sunflower experiment. "First word that pops into your head for each. Go."

"Jaws," said Saad. "Scary movie." For bee he just shrugged. "Honey, I guess."

Lucy turned to Reid. "Now think of someone you actually know who's been stung and had to sit in the office." Reid raised his hand slowly. His little sister, twice. His neighbor. He chewed his marker, then wrote on his sheet: one vivid story is not evidence; a tested claim needs counting, and the counting says I know three sting victims and zero shark victims.

The bell rang before Mr. Rosen could collect the papers, and Reid picked up the crayfish's empty shell to return it to the tank himself. He held his breath the whole way, then grinned at his wet fingers. "Friday," he said. "I'm bringing goggles."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: A top, or apex, predator is at the end of its food chain and, as an adult, has no natural predators of its own.
story:
Ryan spread his poster board across the picnic table and uncapped the markers before anyone could change the subject. "Okay, today we settle it," he announced. "Hawk or owl. Which one's at the top of the chain in the woods behind my house?"

Maiya dropped her bike in the grass and leaned over the board. "You're so gullible," she told Cody, who had been arguing for the owl since Tuesday. "You heard one hoot and decided owls rule the forest."

At the science museum last month, the three of them had stood in front of a wall-sized mural of a forest food web, tracing arrows with their fingers from the sun to the grass to the rabbit to the hawk. Ryan remembered the exact moment the argument started, because Cody had jabbed his finger at a great horned owl painted in the corner and declared, "That thing looks way more dangerous." They had gotten so loud that a guard shuffled over, and they'd left without an answer. Now, in Ryan's backyard with the whole afternoon ahead of them, he intended to get one.

"Watch," Ryan said, and drew the chain in big confident strokes: sun, grass, grasshopper, snake, hawk. He tapped the last arrow. "The hawk's the end. That makes it a top predator. My book calls that an apex predator." He paused, thinking it through out loud. "As an adult, nothing out there hunts it. It has no natural predators of its own. So the hawk is at the top."

"Unless," Cody said slowly, "the owl is also at the top of its own chain. Two ends. Two tops."

They stared at each other. Ryan grabbed a second marker and drew a parallel chain, sun to acorn to mouse to owl, and suddenly the poster had two apexes, and neither arrow pointed at the other. Maiya whooped like they'd won something.

Then came the twist. Mr. Castillo leaned over the fence with a rake in one hand and held up something small and gray with the other. "You three dropped this on the nature trail yesterday," he said. "Found it by the big oak." It was a weathered drawing on notebook paper, unmistakably Ryan's own handwriting: a food chain with the sun at the start and, at the end, a fierce cartoon cat wearing a crown.

"That's not a predator," Cody said. "That's Whiskers."

Ryan's conscience pinched him, because he'd drawn it as a joke in science class and never owned up. He took the paper, then grinned and taped it to the corner of the poster with one last arrow. "Fine. Whiskers is the apex predator of this backyard. Nobody hunts her."

From the porch, the cat yawned and stretched, surveying her kingdom.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago.
story:
Lea spread her notebook across the library table and stared at the empty page. Her assignment was due Friday: explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming. Ms. Koné had said the report had to make sense to someone who knew nothing about Egypt, and Lea's mind felt exactly like someone who knew nothing about Egypt.

She pulled a book from the shelf, one with a cracked spine and a photo of the pyramids on the cover, sand-colored against a pale sky. The pages smelled dusty and faintly of glue. She read that the Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago. She read that the Nile flooded every year, leaving dark mud that made the fields fertile, so farmers could grow wheat in a desert. But the numbers felt like nothing. Four thousand five hundred years might as well have been four million.

Makayla slid into the chair across from her, chewing a straw. "What's the book? What genre even is that?"

"Nonfiction. History." Lea tapped the page. "It says the pyramid is four and a half thousand years old. I can't picture it. My grandmother is seventy."

Makayla squinted. "So?"

"So my grandmother's whole life is seventy years. I want to know how many grandmothers it would take, standing in a line, mothers having daughters, all the way back to when they built it." Lea grabbed a pencil. If each grandmother was born when her mother was about twenty-five, then one lifetime of seventy years covered roughly three generations. She divided 4,500 by seventy and got about sixty-four. Sixty-four grandmothers, hand to hand, back to Khufu.

"That's not that many," Makayla said, leaning over. "Sixty-four people could fit in the gym."

Lea tested the idea a different way. She counted backward by hand on the page, marking each seventy years, and reached the same answer. Then she tried it with lifetimes of sixty years, and the line stretched to seventy-five grandmothers, but the pyramid still stood at the end of it, waiting. Either way, the pyramid was older than every one of those people combined, and it was still there.

She wrote at the top of her page: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago. Below it she started drawing a line of sixty-four stick figures, each one labeled "grandmother," ending at a triangle. The pharaoh wanted something permanent, she wrote, and the farmers who could grow all that grain because of the Nile's yearly flood were the ones who could contribute the food and labor to build it.

Ismail dropped his backpack on the table and peered at the drawing. "Why are there all those little ladies?"

"That's how old the pyramid is," Lea said, and slid the notebook toward him. "Count them yourself."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: The urge to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide in the blood, not by falling oxygen.
story:
Beatrice flopped onto the grass beside the soccer goal, still puffing from her third attempt at the length. In two days she had to swim twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, in front of the whole class, and so far she could not make it past the flags.

"You looked like you were being chased by a shark," said Sylvia, sitting down next to her, "except slower."

"Ha ha." Beatrice winced, thinking of Friday's test. "Halfway down the pool I get so desperate for air that I stand up. Every single time. I don't know what's wrong with me."

Sylvia pulled her water bottle out of her bag. "My cousin's a lifeguard. She says the urge to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide in the blood, not by falling oxygen." She took a swig. "So if you hold your air in, the CO2 builds up and your body panics, even though you've got plenty of oxygen left."

Beatrice sat up. "Wait. So it's not that I need air. It's that I'm hoarding it."

"That's what she said."

"So if I let the air out slowly while my face is down, instead of keeping it all in, the desperate feeling might not come." Beatrice stood, brushed grass off her knees, and decided to be systematic about it. "I'll try three exhales patterns. Bubbles the whole time, bubbles on every second stroke, bubbles on every third. Whichever works, I keep."

At the pool the next afternoon, Serena stood at the deep end with the stopwatch. "Trial one," she called.

Trial one was wobbly, and trial two went off course like a drunk duck, but on trial three, with a long steady stream of bubbles escaping her nose, Beatrice reached the far wall and slapped the tile. She was breathing hard, but she was not desperate.

"Twenty-five metres," Serena announced. "Legal breathing and everything."

Beatrice pushed her goggles up and grinned. "Told you. It was never about the air I needed. It was about the air I was hiding."

"Whatever," said Serena, resetting the watch. "Again."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
Nicolas stared at the group chat on his phone, thumbs hovering. Alexane had posted a link with the words "THIS PROVES IT, tomatoes cause headaches, read the whole thing." The link went to a blog called Wellness Warrior Wanda, written by someone who claimed she had gotten a headache every single time she ate a tomato for two weeks.

Nicolas typed, "But that's just one person. You hate tomatoes anyway. You said they taste like angry water."

"That's not the point," Alexane replied, followed by three angry-face emojis.

"It's kind of the point," Savanna chimed in.

Nicolas flopped onto his bed, phone held above his face, which was a mistake, because the phone dropped on his nose. Rubbing it, he remembered Saturday at the library, three weeks ago. He had been hunting proof that listening to music while doing homework made you worse at homework, because his dad kept saying so. Ms. García, the librarian, had watched him scroll and scroll, and then slid two printouts across the table. One was a blog post by a man who said music wrecked his focus. The other was a paper from a journal, full of charts and a long list of scientists at the end.

"That one looks boring," Nicolas had said.

"That one looks boring because before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors," Ms. García had said. "It's called peer review."

"Scientists checking other scientists?" Nicolas had asked.

"Exactly. The blog? Nobody checked it."

Back on his bed now, Nicolas typed fast. "Ask Ms. García tomorrow. Find a journal article about tomatoes and headaches. If scientists tested a bunch of people and other scientists reviewed the paper for errors, that's actual proof. Wanda's two weeks is just Wanda."

Suspense built in the chat all evening. Alexane sent "..." at 9:02. At 9:14 she sent a photo of a journal article titled "Dietary Triggers and Headache: A Controlled Study of 1,200 Participants," with the words PEER REVIEWED stamped across the top in red pen because she had gotten excited with a marker.

"Oops," she wrote. "Anyway. It says tomatoes are basically fine for most people. Wanda might just get headaches anyway, and blames the tomato."

Nicolas grinned. "So one person's story isn't nothing, but it isn't proof either."

"Fine. You win. I'll still never eat tomatoes. Angry water forever."

The next morning, Savanna brought in a printout with a sticky note that said NICOLAS WAS RIGHT in enormous letters, and Ms. García read the whole chat over their shoulders, verified the article was real, and said, "Cumulative evidence, checked step by step. That's how it works." Nicolas taped the sticky note inside his binder, right under a doodle of Wanda holding a giant suspicious tomato.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Declan spread his survey results across the kitchen table, twenty-eight slips of paper covered in his careful printing. He had asked every kid in his class two questions: did you eat breakfast this morning, and what did you get on the last math quiz? The pattern jumped out at him. Almost all the breakfast eaters had scored 80 or higher, and almost all the kids who skipped it had landed somewhere in the 60s. His poster board read, in fat red letters, "Eating Breakfast Causes Better Grades." He was reaching for the glue when his phone buzzed.

"That's a huge finding," Marissa said from the video call, her face peering out from Declan's propped-up tablet. "But wait. My mom makes eggs for me every morning because she's home before work. Priya's mom works nights, so Priya grabs nothing and rushes out the door." She tapped her chin. "What if the moms are the real difference? Like, the kids with somebody checking on them in the morning also get help with homework."

Declan felt his forehead begin to perspire, the way it did when a project was about to fall apart in his hands. He stared at his poster. If Marissa was right, breakfast might not be causing anything. "So two things going together doesn't prove one causes the other," he said slowly. "Something else could cause both."

"That's called correlation," Marissa said. "We just read about it. It's like hummingbirds showing up wherever the flowers are. The birds don't make the nectar, and the nectar doesn't make the birds. The warm weather brings both."

Declan pulled the red letters off the poster before the glue dried. That was the crucial part, he realized, catching the mistake now instead of at the fair in front of Mr. Cheung and everybody. He wrote a new headline: "Breakfast and Grades: Connected, But Who's Causing What?" Then he added a third survey question for the class: "Does someone help you with homework at home?"

"Better," Marissa said, and read the new poster upside down through the camera. Declan capped the glue stick, lined up his fresh questionnaires, and texted his teacher to save him a bigger table.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In a food chain diagram, the arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy flows.
story:
The waiting room of the veterinary clinic smelled like dog shampoo and coffee, and Brooke spread her science poster across two chairs while her cat, Biscuit, grumbled inside his carrier. Her poster showed a food chain: sun, grass, rabbit, hawk. She had been proud of it until Ms. Walker, the vet tech behind the desk, paused on her way past with a clipboard and said, "Nice hawk. Interesting arrow, though." Then she kept walking, which was not helpful at all.

"What's wrong with my arrow?" Brooke asked. She had drawn one from the hawk to the rabbit, from the rabbit to the grass, from the grass to the sun, so every picture pointed back to the beginning. It looked organized to her. It looked tidy.

Milania, who had come along because her own dog was being weighed and because she wanted, more than anything, to be allowed in the back to watch, leaned over the poster. "Wait. Your grass is eating your rabbit," she said, and then laughed so hard she knocked a brochure rack of flea pamphlets onto the floor. "Look at it. The arrow goes from hawk to rabbit. It's like the grass is eating everything."

Brooke frowned. Why did the direction of an arrow matter so much? She turned a pencil over in her hands and thought about what an arrow usually meant. An arrow points somewhere, from one thing toward another. She looked at her drawing of the hawk and the rabbit and asked herself a quiet question: what actually moves between them, and which way? The rabbit doesn't jump into the hawk's mouth backwards. Something goes from the rabbit into the hawk, and that something is the energy that keeps the hawk hunting. She erased every arrow and redrew them the other way, from the sun to the grass, from the grass to the rabbit, from the rabbit to the hawk.

"The arrows point from the thing that is eaten to the thing that eats it," she said slowly, reading the chain like a sentence. "It shows which way the energy flows." Then a strange thought struck her. "So if I erase the rabbits, what happens to the hawk?" There would be no link, no energy moving upward, nothing to govern how the hawk survived. She imagined the whole chain sagging like a rope with a missing rung.

Milania had stopped laughing. She was tracing the arrows with her finger, frowning at the poster, and being, for once, not biased toward jokes. "Okay, that's actually cool," she admitted. "Do it again but with mice." Ms. Walker passed by on her way to fetch Biscuit, glanced down at the corrected arrows, and gave Brooke a small nod. Milania raised her hand and called out, "Can we watch from the back? Just the weighing part?" Ms. Walker held the door open, and Milania was through it before Brooke had even capped her marker.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
story:
Anthony tapped his pencil against his notebook and counted the words he still had to memorize before Friday. Ms. Sow's German quiz would ask everyone to describe their family in full sentences, and Anthony's family was not built for short answers. He had three brothers, one sister, two dogs, and a hamster named Klaus who bit people. His friend Kiaan had to describe only one cat, which seemed deeply unfair.

"I'm going to run out of paper," Anthony said at lunch, sliding his notebook across the table. "Look. Mein Bruder. Mein Bruder. Mein Bruder. Meine Schwester. That's just the people, and I still have the dogs."

Kiaan leaned over the page, chewing his sandwich. "Kylan says his brother is an exchange student in Hamburg, and the kid has a word for the whole pile." He grinned. "Want to trade lunches for it?"

"That's pessimistic of you, thinking I won't find it myself," Anthony said, but he slid his cookies across the table anyway.

After school, the two of them sat in the computer lab, where Ms. Sow had come to supervise the last study hour. Anthony decided to test the idea like a science experiment. He opened the class German vocabulary database and typed in "siblings." One result popped up: Geschwister. He said it out loud three times, then wrote a trial sentence. Ich habe vier Geschwister. Four words instead of eight, and it covered all his brothers and his sister in one sweep, the way "siblings" did in English.

"It works," he announced. "Geschwister. Kiaan, it's a two-cookie word and you only charged me one."

Kylan, passing by on his way out, looked at the screen and laughed. "Told you. My brother uses it every week on the phone."

Anthony wrote his full description one more time, folded the paper into a paper airplane, and sailed it across the room. "Das ist meine Familie," he said, "Klaus included."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, clicking the green flag starts every script that begins with 'when green flag clicked', and the red stop sign stops all scripts.
story:
Olivier had built the whole game: a cat that chased a bouncing ball, a loop that moved the ball forever, and an if-then block that added a point to the score whenever the cat touched it. He pressed the green flag at the top of the screen and waited. Nothing moved. He clicked it again, harder, as if the extra force might help.

"Yours won't start either?" said Frank from the next computer. His shark game showed the same frozen stage. Claudia leaned over from her seat, chewing the end of her stylus. She pointed at Olivier's script area, where his stack of blocks sat there solid and tidy with nothing on top of it. Her own script had a rounded yellow block that said "when green flag clicked" sitting above everything, like a hat.

Olivier dragged his blocks apart and pulled the yellow hat block from the blocks palette, clicking it onto the top of his stack. Then he pressed the green flag again. The ball sprang into its loop, bouncing edge to edge, and when the cat caught it, the score changed from zero to one. "It works," he said, and then, quieter, "Every script needs the hat. That's the rule." He looked over at Frank's screen. "You're missing it too."

Frank found his own hat block, and his shark began swimming in circles. But it would not stop, even after Frank clicked back to the stage to admire it. The shark kept circling, faster and faster, until Frank laughed and covered his eyes. Olivier remembered the red stop sign beside the green flag, the button he had pressed once at the very start out of curiosity, when everything had gone still at once. "Try the stop sign," he said. "The red one stops all scripts." Frank clicked it, and the shark froze mid-circle.

Mr. Dela Cruz came by and looked at the score on Olivier's screen, now at fourteen. "Nice loop," he said, and gave a thumbs up. Olivier realized his insight had been consistent all along: the green flag started everything, and the red sign ended it, and between those two buttons his whole game lived. He nudged Claudia's elbow and pointed at her screen, where her if-then block was set to the wrong variable. "Your score's going up when it should go down," he said. "Wanna check yours together?"

Claudia grinned and rolled her chair closer. "Race you to fifty points."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf prices usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till; in the UK and EU, shown prices already include VAT.
story:
Willow counted the money one more time before she left the house: two dollars and ninety-nine cents, exactly what the milk cost on the shelf at the corner store. Her mother had said she could go alone this time, and the coins felt heavy and important in her pocket, like they could propel her the whole three blocks.

At the till, the cashier scanned the carton and said, "Three dollars and nineteen cents, please." Willow stared at her handful of coins. She was twenty cents short, and the shelf had clearly said two ninety-nine. She felt her face go hot. Behind her, her friend Nada popped up with a basket of her own, and Willow whispered the problem to her.

"It said two ninety-nine," Willow said. "I checked twice."

"Maybe the tag was for a different size?" Nada suggested.

Willow shook her head. Then she remembered last summer, when her cousin in England had visited and bought crisps at the same store. "Wait," Willow said slowly. "My cousin kept saying our prices were a lie. At home in the UK, the price on the shelf is the price you pay. Here it's not. Here they add the tax at the till, so the tag is never the whole story." That was the hidden thing, the reason her exact coins were not enough.

"Here, I have a quarter," Nada said, sliding it across. "You can pay me back Monday."

Willow paid, and the cashier counted the change out loud, coin by coin. Willow counted it again herself, twice, the way her mother had taught her, and got seventeen cents back. She would owe Nada eight cents and still have money left from her allowance. On the walk home she decided to test her idea: she turned the milk carton over and found the nutrition label, where the words carbohydrate and calcium sat in tidy rows. Numbers on packages, she thought, could be ambiguous; you had to know which ones counted and when.

She carried the milk past Ms. Bélanger's porch, where the neighbour was watering her geraniums. "First solo mission?" Ms. Bélanger asked.

"Milk secured," Willow said, holding up the carton like a trophy. "And I'm bringing an extra quarter next time."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: Breathing every three strokes makes a swimmer breathe on alternate sides, because an odd number of arm strokes switches which arm is recovering.
story:
Amelia gripped the pool edge and counted the flags snapping above the water. Only two days until Friday, when Mr. Kaya would watch every kid swim twenty-five metres of front crawl, and she still couldn't finish a lap without swallowing half the pool. Allan and Tucker were already zooming down the lanes beside her like torpedo eels.

"Watch me breathe," Allan called, powering past with his head turning neatly to the side. "Mr. Kaya says I only breathe on my right, though. I always end up over by the rope."

Amelia pushed off and tried it herself: one arm, two arms, breathe right, again breathe right. Halfway down the lane she smacked straight into the lane rope, and Tucker had to haul her off it, laughing so hard he nearly sank. Then she noticed something. Tucker, who breathed right, then left, then right, was swimming dead straight. Allan, who breathed right, right, right, drifted left every single lap, always left, never right, like a ferry on a fixed route.

She hauled herself out and stood dripping at the end of Tucker's lane, thinking so hard her goggles fogged. Tucker was taking three strokes between breaths. Three. If she counted her own strokes, one, two, three, breathe, then her next breath would come on the other side. Breathing every three strokes had to mean breathing on alternate sides, because an odd number of arm strokes switched which arm was recovering when she turned to breathe. That was why Allan curved off course, breathing on one side only. She couldn't see the pattern underwater, but she could test it.

"Tucker, call out my strokes," she said, snapping her goggles back on. "I'll breathe every three, no matter what."

"Today's cuisine at the snack bar is hot dogs and regret," Tucker announced, "but tomorrow it's victory nachos, so pass that test." She kicked off, counting silently. Three strokes, breathe left. Three more, breathe right. Left, right, left, right, all the way down the lane, and the wall of the far end met her hands exactly where it should.

She looked back up the lane she had swum. Straight as a ruler. Behind her, Allan was trying it too, and even from a distance she could hear his whoop. Mr. Kaya, watching from the diving block, gave her a single thumbs up and pointed at the clock, as if to say the water was hers. On Friday, she thought, and she dove straight back in.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.
story:
Alice had been dreading lunch all morning, because Ziad and Yaseen were still angry at each other over the group project, and Ms. Rajapakse had asked her to sit with them and help sort it out. Last year she had tried the same thing with two other kids and it had gone badly; she had taken her friend's side immediately, and the other girl had never really spoken to her again. She kept thinking about that as she carried her tray toward the corner table.

"I'm not sitting near him," Ziad said, arms folded, looking defiant.

"You didn't do your part, that's all I said," Yaseen shot back.

Alice raised her hands. "Before we talk about the project, I want rules for the conversation itself." She had read a page in the library about mediators the night before, and one line had stuck with her: mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.

"Rules?" Ziad said. "Like ground rules?"

"Right. One at a time, and no name-calling. You both have to agree before we start." She slid a napkin across the table. "Write your names on it if you agree."

Ziad wrote his name first, then Yaseen, which surprised her. When Yaseen began to explain that he'd done the slides alone and the research alone, Ziad opened his mouth, caught Alice's eye, and closed it again. He waited. When it was his turn, he said the reason he hadn't done his part was that his grandmother had been in the hospital and he hadn't wanted anyone to know. Yaseen's shoulders dropped.

"Okay," Alice said, and she drew two stick figures on the napkin to depict them shaking hands. They didn't actually shake hands. But by the time the bell rang, they had reached a consensus to redo the slides together, and Ziad asked her, "Same table tomorrow?"

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
Gemma shoved her phone across the carpet and refused to look at it. "It's gone," she said. "I deleted it last night, the second I woke up."

Alice picked it up anyway. On the screen was Gemma's old club blog, the public one their whole grade had found in September, still showing the post where Gemma had called the science fair judges "clueless zombies." At least, Alice was almost sure it did. She tapped the address into her own borrowed phone and the page loaded fresh, without it.

"See?" Gemma said. "Deleted means deleted."

But Alice had a funny intuition about that, the same feeling she got when a magic trick obviously had a trick to it. Public things on the internet felt different from private texts. A text vanished into your phone. A blog post had been sitting out in the open where anyone, anything, could walk by and look at it. What if something out there had been looking, and remembering?

"I hypothesize there's an old copy somewhere," she said, typing. "A place that saves pages. My brother mentioned it once, when the school site went down."

She searched: archive of old web pages. A result came up right away, the Wayback Machine, with a search box and a claim on the screen that made her blink. Saved web pages: more than one trillion.

"No way," Gemma said, leaning over despite herself.

Alice pasted in the blog's address and hit the button. A little calendar appeared, full of dates. She picked one from before last night, before the deletion. The page rebuilt itself on the screen, slow and slightly wrong-looking, like a counterfeit version of the original, but there it was. The zombie line, word for word, in Gemma's own font.

Gemma groaned and dropped her forehead onto the carpet.

"Okay," Alice said, already wondering how many of her own deleted posts lived in there. "So what do we do about it?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
Aiden had been chosen to welcome the new student, and he still hadn't decided how. Ms. Fernando had said on Friday, "You can delegate jobs if you like, but the welcome itself is yours," which meant everyone would be watching him. He'd planned a handshake, the kind his grandfather taught him: firm, two pumps, then let go. That was good manners in his house.

The new student, Louis-Felix, arrived on Tuesday morning with a small wrapped parcel in his hands. Aiden noticed the tag said his own name, so Louis-Felix must have known he'd be the welcomer. "In France we bring something," Louis-Felix said, holding it out. "It would be strange not to." Aiden took it with both hands because somehow that felt right, and slid it into his desk, unsure whether opening it now would be rude or not opening it would be rude. Renee leaned over and whispered, "At my grandma's you open it right away so she knows you like it." He decided to wait, and watch.

Then the room went quiet because Ms. Fernando had stood up. "Louis-Felix lived in New Zealand for two years before this school," she said, "and he has something to show us." Louis-Felix turned to Aiden. "I want to do it properly," he said. "In New Zealand, when someone new arrives, there's a greeting called a hongi." He stepped close and pressed his nose and forehead gently against Aiden's. Aiden held still, surprised by how warm it was. "It means we share the breath of life," Louis-Felix said softly, and stepped back.

At lunch Aiden sat across from Louis-Felix and worked something out between bites. His mother said elbows off the table; Renee's family ate with bread torn by hand; Louis-Felix kept his fork upside down in his left fist, European style, and seemed comfortable. So the rules weren't one big rule, Aiden thought. They were more like a ratio, a few parts each family and each country mixed in its own way. No wonder the gullible kids in class believed there was only one correct way to do everything.

He tried his theory out. "Watch," he told Renee, and turned to Louis-Felix. "Do it again, the greeting. I want to get it right this time." Louis-Felix smiled, leaned in, and their noses and foreheads touched. Behind them, Renee whispered, "Okay, now I want one too."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Sarah's phone buzzed at exactly four o'clock, which meant she had two hours before the online deal on VoltBerry vanished at midnight and only one hour before her mom picked her up from Soraya's house. Soraya had the website open on her laptop, and it looked amazing. A sleek blue page, a photo of a smiling runner, and big letters promising that VoltBerry Focus Drink improved concentration in nine out of ten kids.

"I have forty dollars from my birthday," Soraya said, drumming her fingers on the desk. "That's almost enough for the six-bottle pack. It would help with the spelling bee on Friday for sure."

Sarah leaned closer. The site was full of testimonials from people named things like "Verified Mom of 3" and even a quote from somebody calling himself Dr. Halversen, Expert in Nutrition. It all sounded convincing right up until Sarah scrolled to the bottom and found a tiny line: VoltBerry Wellness Group. A thought tickled at her. The website was saying wonderful things about itself, which was a bit like asking a magician whether his trick was real. She couldn't see who was behind the page just by reading the page.

"Can I borrow your laptop for a second?" she asked. She opened a new tab and typed VoltBerry Wellness Group into a search engine. The first result was a news article from last spring: VoltBerry Wellness Group was the company that made the drink. The same company. A second article mentioned that Dr. Halversen, Expert in Nutrition, was actually the company's founder. A third, from a science teacher's blog, called the concentration claims "corrosive nonsense that erodes kids' trust in real nutrition." Soraya's mouth dropped open.

"So the website reviewing the drink and the company selling the drink are one and the same," Soraya said slowly. "That's a straight-up contradiction. They pretend it's an outside opinion."

"My cousin calls that lateral reading," Sarah said. "Instead of judging a site by its own pages, you open new tabs and see what other sources say about it." It made sense to Sarah the way a rule made sense: once you knew it, you couldn't un-know it. She opened one more tab and found an actual university study on berry drinks. Nothing about concentration, nothing about nine out of ten kids. That eliminated the last shred of her doubt.

Soraya closed the laptop with a firm click. "Forty dollars stays in my drawer," she said. "And on Friday, I'm just going to study the old-fashioned way."

Sarah grinned and checked the time. "Race you to practice the word 'preliminary' before my mom gets here."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Sarah's family reunion started at four, and dinner was at six sharp, because Auntie insisted the noodles be eaten hot. Sarah had one job before dinner: look after her little cousins on the back porch. She could hear the grown-ups inside, laughing over plates, someone recounting the story of the year Grandma's pie collapsed. Out on the porch, the youngest cousin, a round-faced boy of four, kept climbing onto the railing.

Lilyanna from next door had been invited too, since her family knew Sarah's aunt from years back. Lilyanna arrived with a small wrapped box, which confused Sarah, because Sarah's family hadn't brought gifts. "We always bring something," Lilyanna said. "It's just what we do." Sarah filed that away.

The boy on the railing wobbled. Sarah darted over and caught his arm, and in relief she reached out to ruffle his hair, the way her dad did to her. Lilyanna's hand shot out, not quite grabbing Sarah's wrist, but close. "Wait, don't touch his head."

Sarah froze. "Why not?" She looked at the boy, who was giggling, entirely fine.

"In Thailand, the head is sacred," Lilyanna said. "Touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be rude. His mom's from Bangkok. She's really nice about stuff, but I wouldn't."

Sarah's cheeks went warm. She tried to think back through the afternoon. Had she patted anyone's head already? She remembered steadying the boy once before, near the drinks table, and she could not recall whether her hand had landed on his shoulder or higher. That was the hidden part, the thing she couldn't see directly. She needed a way to find out.

"Watch the railing for a second," she told Lilyanna, and she carried the boy inside on her hip, keeping her hands firmly on his back. His mother was slicing mango near the sink. "Excuse me," Sarah said. "Earlier, by the drinks, I might have touched his head. I just found out that in Thailand the head is sacred, and I'm sorry if I did."

His mother smiled and rinsed her knife. "You are very kind to ask. Maybe you touched his shoulder, maybe not. Either way, he likes you." She offered Sarah a slice of mango on a saucer, and Sarah took it with both hands, the way Lilyanna had taken the noodles earlier, and that felt right too.

Back on the porch, the sun sat low over the fence, and the smell of noodles drifted out through the screen door. Six o'clock was twenty minutes off. Lilyanna raised an eyebrow at the mango. "Plausible plan," Sarah said, "apologizing before you know you did anything wrong." She sat down on the steps, and the little boy climbed into the space beside her, careful this time to keep both feet on the boards.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
Anais spread her science fair board across the kitchen table and frowned at the empty middle panel. Her experiment had gone fine. She had filled three bowls with water, left one plain, added salt to the second, and sugar to the third, then frozen them overnight to see which one turned to ice first. The plain water had frozen solid, the sugar water was mushy, and the salt water was still stubbornly liquid, like an obstinate classmate refusing to line up. But the top of the board needed a word she kept seeing in the instruction sheet: hypothesis. She had skipped over it all week, the way she skipped over the word "stanza" in poetry until Mr. Karimi made her class memorize what one was. Now she was stuck.

She called London, who was no help at all. "Just write what you guessed," London said through the phone. "I despise those vocabulary words. Write 'I guessed the salt water would freeze last' and glue it down."

"That's not the same as a hypothesis, though," Anais said. "The sheet wants the exact word." She hung up, dragged the dictionary off the shelf, and looked it up herself. The entry said the word came from ancient Greek. It literally meant "putting or placing under."

She sat back. "Placing under," she said out loud to the empty kitchen. She thought of her mother placing a rug under a wobbly table leg, something slid underneath to hold the whole thing up. That was what a guess did. You put it under your experiment first, before you knew anything, and the experiment either held it up or knocked it flat. Her guess had been that salt water would freeze last, and the freezer had agreed with her. The guess had been placed under, and the evidence stood on top of it.

She wrote HYPOTHESIS in big blue letters across the panel, and under it: Salt water will freeze last. Then she carried the board to the living room to show her mother, holding it the way you hold something that finally makes sense.

"Look," she said. "The word goes underneath everything."

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: Flour thickens a sauce because its starch grains soak up liquid and swell when heated, so the sauce thickens as it comes up to a simmer.
story:
The recipe card came from Ms. Kapoor next door, and Victoria had promised macaroni and cheese for dinner at six o'clock, when her mother got home from her shift. At five fifteen she had a pot of milk, a knob of butter, and a whisk, and by five thirty she had a smooth paste of butter and flour bubbling in the pan. That part, the roux, had gone fine. She poured in the warm milk a splash at a time, whisking like Ms. Kapoor had shown her through the fence, and for one shining moment the sauce looked like liquid silk.

Then it looked like milk. Thin, pale, watery milk. Victoria whisked harder, but the sauce stayed stubbornly runny, and the minutes on the clock seemed to dwindle faster than the liquid in the pot. At five forty she reached for the flour tin. Eve, who had come over to watch and steal cheese cubes, leaned on the counter. "If you add more flour you'll get lumps again," she said. "Remember the first batch? Little dough balls everywhere."

Victoria set the tin down and stared at the pot. The first batch had been lumpy when she dumped cold flour straight into hot milk. This batch was different, because the flour had already gone in, cooked in the butter, every grain coated. She thought about the rice in Ms. Kapoor's pudding, how each grain swelled up fat and soft as it drank the liquid. Maybe the flour grains in her sauce were doing the same thing, soaking up milk and swelling, and maybe that took heat and time. Nothing had told her that yet, because the pot wasn't hot enough.

"So the sauce thickens as it comes up to a simmer," Victoria said slowly, "not the second the flour goes in." She turned the burner up a notch, kept whisking, and waited. Slowly, the milk began to steam, small bubbles formed at the edges, and the sauce thickened under her whisk into something glossy and substantial. She pulled it off the heat, stirred in a big handful of cheddar until it melted in smooth ropes, and tasted it. Her one criterion for tonight was simple: no lumps. There were none.

At six o'clock exactly, her mother walked in the door, sniffed, and smiled. Eve was already setting out three bowls. "Macaroni and cheese," Victoria announced, carrying the pot to the table with both hands. "From scratch. And I only ruined it once."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
story:
Chloe had signed up to volunteer at the community food bank because Mr. Kamau said it counted for two hours of service credit, and because she imagined handing bags of groceries to people who needed them. On Saturday morning she stood in the middle of a huge warehouse, shelves reaching to the ceiling, pallets of canned beans stacked in rows like buildings. She waited by the door with her friend Sylas. Nobody came in.

"Maybe people sleep late on Saturdays," Sylas said.

They waited forty more minutes. A forklift beeped past. Chloe counted the doorways: one for deliveries at the back, one for volunteers, and none marked for visitors at all. That was the clue. A place with no checkout counter and no visitor entrance wasn't built for people to shop in. She walked to the loading dock and read the labels on the outgoing crates. Every box was stamped with the name of a church, a school, or a community center, and one word kept appearing: pantry.
