"So this is a warehouse," she said slowly. "A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food. The pantries are the local places where people actually pick it up. Like the one on Miller Street." She pointed at a crate. "We're the behind-the-scenes part."

A woman with a clipboard, who managed the floor, overheard her. "Smart kid. Want to help load the Miller Street run? That driver's trying to conquer a whole route before noon."

Chloe carried boxes until her arms ached. The woman talked while they worked, about how she'd started here years ago after her house went into mortgage trouble and a pantry had fed her family for a winter. She said she wasn't biased toward any one pantry, but Miller Street was her favorite because they never let anyone leave with an empty cart.

Then the van door rolled up, and Chloe froze. Climbing into the passenger seat was Sylas's older brother, and stacked beside him, waiting to carry the boxes in, was Macey, holding a shopping bag from Miller Street.

"Don't tell anyone," Macey said, and held up the bag. "Saturday's our day."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Jace had promised his grandmother he would make dinner tonight, chicken and a big salad, and he'd been planning it since Tuesday. The kitchen at her house smelled like cinnamon and old newspapers, and the wooden cutting board by the sink had a scratch down the middle that he ran his thumb over while he thought. First he cubed the raw chicken, then he washed his hands, then he reached for the lettuce. His hand stopped halfway.

Wait, he thought. The board still had chicken juices in that scratch, maybe, or somewhere he couldn't see. If he chopped lettuce on it, whatever was on the lettuce would be eaten raw, straight onto everyone's plates. Nobody cooked salad. So whatever the raw chicken left behind would ride along, invisible, right into his grandmother and his little cousin. Was that a thing with a name? He'd heard a word once in a video at school. "Cross-contamination," he said out loud, testing it. The spread of bacteria from one food to another. That had to be it.

He was a little skeptical of himself, though. Was he being too careful? His friend Shania would say he was overthinking it, but Shania had once eaten a sandwich off the floor of the gym. The rule, if it was a rule, seemed simple: use separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad. He could test it without any fancy equipment. If using the same board was such a bad idea, then the clean board in the cupboard was the obvious candidate for the lettuce. Switching boards would violate nothing except his habit of doing dishes only once. He pulled out the fresh board and set it down with a clack.

His grandmother came in, drying her hands on her apron. "Two boards tonight?"

"One for the chicken, one for the salad," Jace said. "Cross-contamination. You can't see it happen, so you have to stop it before it does."

She looked at the scratched board, then at him, and pulled a third board out of the cupboard for the tomatoes.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
David spread his science fair notebook across the library table and frowned at the page. His experiment was supposed to prove that the plant food he had bought actually made bean plants grow taller, but his three sprouts in the kitchen window had all shot up about the same amount, fed or not. He was missing something, and the librarian had pointed him to a shelf of experiment books near the window.

Moses slid into the chair across from him, balancing a stack of books about volcanoes. "Still stuck on the bean thing?" he asked. David turned the notebook around so Moses could see the chart. Each plant had gotten the plant food mixed into its water, just at different strengths, and every row showed nearly identical heights. "If the food works," Moses said slowly, "shouldn't one of them look different?"

David stared at the chart, and an uneasy feeling sharpened into an acute suspicion: maybe all three plants were getting something that made them grow, which would make them look the same even if the food worked. He flipped to an experiment in one of the library books about testing fertilizer on bean plants, and there it was. The diagram showed tested plants, and beside them one extra pot that got no fertilizer at all. He read the label twice. "That one just gets plain water," he said. "Nothing added. It's called a control group."

Chelsey, who had been listening from the next table while she searched the catalog, leaned over. "So how does that help you?" David picked up his pencil and drew a fourth pot on his chart, labeled plain water only. Now, whatever happened to that plant would show him how tall beans grew anyway, and he could compare the others against it. "Without it," he said, "my whole project just proves that bean plants grow, which nobody needs to prove."

Mr. Tang, shelving books two aisles over, had drifted closer and nodded at the diagram. The three of them reached a quick consensus that David would start four fresh beans tomorrow and document their heights every single morning in the notebook. Moses helped him copy the watering schedule onto a clean page, and Chelsey found him a book about roots.

That evening, David set four new pots on the kitchen windowsill, spacing them evenly in the light. He filled the watering can and touched the pencil to the first line of his new chart, ready to document day one. "Grow," he told the little pots, and turned on the tap.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Dissolving salt in water is a physical change, because evaporating the water leaves the same salt behind.
story:
Keira set two jars on the windowsill in Mr. Jung's science room: one with plain water, one with water and a spoonful of salt stirred into it until the salt disappeared. The problem was the quiz on Friday. She had mixed up melting and rusting twice already, and Mr. Jung had written "physical or chemical?" beside a drawing of a burning candle, which she had answered wrong both times. She needed a way to tell them apart that she could actually see, or at least mostly see.

"Salt water," Alivia said, leaning over the jars. "That one looks like nothing happened at all."

"That's the point," Keira said. "If dissolving the salt is a physical change, the salt is still in there, just hiding. If it's a chemical change, something new got made, and the salt is gone forever."

"So how do you find hiding salt?" asked Alexe, who had come over to watch.

Keira thought about the pond behind the school, a tranquil little ecosystem where the water shrank every hot week of summer and left rings of minerals on the rocks. Water could leave. Things left behind stayed behind. "We wait for the water to leave on its own," she said. "Sun's on this window all afternoon."

She taped a label to each jar with the date and put a pencil mark at the water line. For three days the marks crept lower. Alivia checked the plain jar and found nothing at the bottom. On Thursday the salt jar was nearly dry, and Keira scraped the bottom with a spoon. White crystals came up, gritty and square-edged, exactly like the salt from the shaker.

"It came back," Alexe said.

"Dissolving salt in water is a physical change," Keira said, holding out the spoon. "The water left, and the same salt stayed behind."

On Friday, beside the drawing of the candle, she wrote chemical, and thought of smoke that never comes back, and salt that always does. Mr. Jung circled it, and Keira folded the quiz into her pocket with the little crystal still in it, sharp against her fingertip.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
The waiting room at the eyeglasses store smelled like plastic and lemon cleaner, and Livia sat between her mom and a rack of frames, still not used to the idea that the world had been blurry for two years without her noticing. Ms. Do, who owned the shop and did the fittings, had shown her the letters on the chart, and now Livia knew why reading had drifted to arm's length, why the whiteboard at school dissolved into smudges unless she sat in front. Near things were blurry. Far things were fine. She kept turning that over, because it felt backwards from what she'd assumed.

Coen had come along because his mom was picking up his new frames too. His glasses, the old pair, made his eyes look small, like pebbles under glass. Livia had never thought about that before, but she thought about it now while Ms. Do fitted a trial frame on her face and swung the mirror around.

"Whoa," Livia said. Her eyes looked enormous. She leaned closer and they got bigger still, like they belonged to some other girl. "Coen, look. Yours make your eyes small and mine make mine huge. Why?"

Coen shrugged and peered at her over his pebble eyes. "Different problem, probably. I can't see far. You can't see near."

Ms. Do permitted them one guess each before she'd say anything, which was her way with kids who liked to figure things out. Livia held up two fingers, one behind the other, and squinted at the wall of frames across the room. With the trial lenses on, she could read the tiny price tags. Without them, she couldn't read her own hand. So the glasses were bending light somehow, pulling it back into focus. She remembered the poster in the exam room, the little cross-section of an eye, the arrow of light landing short or long. Hers landed behind the mark. The lens had to bend it forward, and a lens that bent light inward, thick in the middle, would magnify. That had to be it.

"Convex," Livia said, mostly to herself. "Mine are convex. Thick in the middle. That's why my eyes look big."

"That's the one," Ms. Do said, and handed her a case.

They walked out into an arid, blowing afternoon, and Livia stopped on the sidewalk because she could see individual leaves on the tree across the street, and every crack in the pavement, all at once. She remembered deciding, back in the fall, not to tell her mom about the blurry pages, because she'd been afraid of looking broken. Maybe that had been a mistake. Maybe she'd just needed one more week. She didn't decide, and the climax of the whole thing, she decided, was this exact moment on the sidewalk anyway.

Coen pointed at the bus stop sign down the block and read it out loud, proving his new pair worked too.

"Race you to the sign," Livia said, and ran.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Showering with soap, especially after exercise, washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor.
story:
Daniel slid into his seat in science class and immediately noticed something strange. Marwa, who usually sat half a foot away, had scooted her chair until it almost touched the desk behind her. Mayson leaned toward the window, pretending the parking lot was fascinating.

"You okay?" Daniel asked Mayson.

"Fine," Mayson said, eyes still on the cars. "Great view today."

Daniel had skipped his shower that morning, and again after basketball practice the night before. He'd been in a rush both times, and he figured skipping once or twice couldn't matter that much. Now, though, a suspicion crept over him like a shadow. He sniffed the collar of his shirt. His whole body went hot.

At lunch, he cornered Mayson by the vending machines. "Be honest. Is it me?"

Mayson looked at the floor, then at the ceiling, then finally at Daniel. "It's you. You smell like a gym sock that got left in a locker over summer break."

"Practice was only last night!"

"Exactly," Mayson said, and somehow that one word made Daniel feel like he'd failed a test he didn't know he was taking.

That night, Daniel turned detective in his own bathroom. He thought about it like a science experiment, the kind Mr. Farah made them write up. Something invisible had to be causing the smell, because he couldn't see anything. Sweat, he decided. But wait, he thought, fresh sweat had never bothered anybody. It was old sweat, sweat that sat around overnight, that turned disgusting. Something was happening to it after it left his skin.

He tested his idea the next morning. He showered with soap, scrubbed everywhere twice, and even used the deodorant his mom had bought and left on the shelf like it was some kind of obligation he was supposed to figure out on his own. He put it on, feeling strangely assertive about it, like a knight putting on armor.

At school, Marwa sat at her normal distance. Mayson leaned back in his chair instead of toward the window. Nobody said anything, which was the whole point.

"So it was sweat all along," Daniel said at lunch. "Sweat sitting around gets gross. Wash it off, no smell."

"Congratulations," Mayson said. "You solved the mystery of yourself."

After practice that afternoon, Daniel was first in line for the showers, towel over his shoulder like a victory flag. He was so fast that Marwa, waiting for the gym exit, called out, "Did you run here?"

"Basically," Daniel shouted back, and pushed open the locker room door.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
story:
Brayden slid his phone across the dinner table so his dad could see the ad glowing on the screen. "It says these shoes change lives," he said. "Change lives. It's like the fourth ad this week that says that."

His dad forked up some rice and squinted at it. "Maybe they do."

"Change them how?" Brayden asked. "By how much? If I bought them and my life didn't change, could anybody prove the ad was wrong?" He thought about Mr. Pereira, his science teacher, who had made the whole class write predictions last spring that could be checked. Brayden had written his prediction wrong on purpose, just to be funny, and still felt a little hot about it when he remembered. Mr. Pereira hadn't laughed. He had just said, "Wrong is fine. Uncheckable is not."

His little sister banged her spoon, contagious in her giggling, and their mom shushed her with a smile. "What are you worked up about, Brayden?"

"The ad makes a claim, sort of, but it's not a claim you could ever test. If a shoe ad said they last two years, I could wait two years and see. If it said they're the lightest shoe under twenty dollars, someone could weigh them and check the price. But 'changes lives'?" He waved a hand. "It gives you nothing to test. Ever. Even if you wore them for fifty years, the company could just say your life changed in some way you didn't notice."

"So don't buy them," his dad said.

"I'm not buying them. I'm going to boycott them and tell Colton and Imogen why. Colton already ordered a pair." Brayden pulled the phone back and started typing a message to Colton: How would you ever know if they were lying? His sister leaned over and tapped the screen with her sticky finger, adding a row of letter j's to the end.

"Send it like that," she said.

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: Both sprint hurdle races, the men's 110 metres and the women's 100 metres, have ten hurdles.
story:
Eve had signed up for the voluntary hurdle clinic at the community pool, mostly because it met on the grass strip beside the deck and she was already there every afternoon anyway. Now she stood in the sprinkler smell of wet chlorine and cut grass, staring at a row of low hurdles that her classmate Ilyes had dragged out of the equipment shed. Ms. Pierre, who coached on Tuesdays, had told them to run the row with a three-step rhythm, but Eve had clipped the third hurdle twice in a row, and the second time she had landed hard enough on her palms that the whole deck went quiet.

"That's it," she said, sitting in the grass. "I'm quitting in front of an audience. This is maximum humiliation."

"You're fine," Ilyes said, though he was frowning at the hurdles, not at her. "Honestly, I don't think it's you."

Eve looked up. "What do you mean?"

"I mean I counted them when I set them up, and something's off." He walked the row, tapping each hurdle. "Seven. Ms. Pierre said a real race row should be ten, because both sprint hurdle races, the men's 110 metres and the women's 100 metres, have ten hurdles. We're three short." He wanted a full race row to practice on before Saturday, she knew, so he could film the whole thing for his track channel.

Eve stood, brushed grass off her knees, and thought about it. If the row was short, maybe Ilyes had squeezed the hurdles closer together to fit them in the same stretch of grass. That would explain her third-hurdle clip better than any clumsiness of hers. You couldn't see wrong spacing just by looking, but you could measure it with your feet. She walked heel-to-toe from the start to the first hurdle, counted, then walked between the first and second, and then the second and third. The third gap was short by almost a full foot.

"Move this one back," she said, hauling the third hurdle down the grass. "It's not me. It's the spacing."

They re-set the whole row, ten hurdles long, stretching it toward the pool fence. Caylee, dripping from the deep end, came over to hold hurdles steady while Eve lined them up. Then Eve backed up to the start, breathed, and ran. One, two, three, lead leg up and over. One, two, three, over again. The third hurdle passed under her knee like it was nothing, and the fourth, and the rest, all the way to the fence, where she stopped with her hands on her head, laughing.

"Get the camera," Ilyes shouted, already running for his backpack. "Ten hurdles, one take."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Theo had planned to build the same volcano every kid built, the brown lump that oozed foam down its sides while everyone pretended to be amazed. But Monica had already claimed volcanoes at lunch, loudly, and Ms. Njoroge had a rule about duplicate projects. So Theo sat at the kitchen table with a baking soda box, a jug of vinegar, and a plan he hoped would be better: measure whether more vinegar meant a bigger eruption, and turn the whole thing into a chart.

He set out five clear cups on the table, each with exactly the same small spoonful of baking soda. The label on the box said sodium bicarbonate, which Theo copied onto his data sheet because it looked scientific. The vinegar bottle said acetic acid. He copied that too. Then he lined up the cups like a little army and got his measuring cup from the mudroom, since his mother had made him promise not to use her good glass ones again.

The first test went badly. He poured a whole cup of vinegar in at once, the foam shot up over the rim, and it pooled across the table and dripped onto his sock. His mother walked by with laundry and did not stop, which was how he knew she had decided it was not her problem. Theo mopped up with a dish towel, then sat still and thought. The liquid was opaque once the fizz clouded it, so he could not see whether the baking soda had fully reacted underneath. He could not watch the hidden cause. He would have to judge it by the effect instead, which meant careful pouring and careful counting.

Eleanor knocked on the door halfway through cup three, drawn by the smell like a scavenger sniffing out snacks. She found none, so she sat down to watch instead. "What's actually happening in there?" she asked, chin on her hands.

"Baking soda, which is sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, which is acetic acid, and it produces carbon dioxide gas," Theo said, reading off his sheet. "The gas is what pushes the foam up."

"That's it? Gas?"

"Gas," Theo said, "and measurement."

Cup two got twice the vinegar of cup one, cup three got three times, and so on down the line, with Theo counting seconds of fizzing and Eleanor calling out when the foam crossed a rubber band he had stretched around each cup as a flood line. The numbers climbed in a pattern so tidy that Theo checked them twice. More acid, more gas, taller foam. He was still graphing it at the table, tongue out, when Monica texted to ask whether he was going to copy her volcano after all.

Theo typed back one word, held the phone up so Eleanor could see, and pressed send. "Jealous."

activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
knowledge_domain: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
fact: In perspective, a circle seen at an angle, such as a round rug on the floor, is drawn as an ellipse, a flattened oval.
story:
Daniel pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the tip snapped, which did not help his mood. Mr. Delgado had promised that anyone who finished a full room in two-point perspective, with two vanishing points off the edges of the page, could hang the drawing in the hallway display case. Daniel wanted that spot. His friend Kody had already drawn a sophisticated-looking living room with a fireplace and tall windows, and every time Kody leaned over to peek at Daniel's page, it irritated Daniel like a fly at a picnic.

"Your walls look great," Kody said, which was fine. "But your rug is weird."

Daniel looked at the round rug in the middle of his floor. He had drawn it as a circle, same as always, and now that he stared at it, the thing looked like a flat sticker pasted on the page instead of a rug lying flat on the floor. The walls receded toward their vanishing points. The rug just sat there, refusing to cooperate.

Akram wandered over from the supply shelf, eating a pretzel rod like a professor with a cigar. "Hmm," he said. "That rug is embarrassing the whole drawing."

"Thanks," said Daniel. But he kept looking at the rug, turning the idea over. The floor slanted away from him in the picture. A round thing sitting on a slanted floor would not show all of itself at once. He remembered the big clock on the far wall, which he had flattened into a narrow oval, and something clicked. He picked up a fresh pretzel rod from Akram without asking and held it flat, level with his eye, then tilted it slowly back. From the side it was a line. Tilted, it flattened into an oval. A circle seen at an angle got squashed.

"So the rug is a circle I'm seeing at an angle," Daniel said. He erased the round rug and drew a flattened oval instead, wider than it was tall, sitting snug between the lines of the floorboards. The rug sank into the room like it belonged there.

"An ellipse," Akram announced, pointing. "That's the word. A flattened oval." Kody groaned and grabbed his own eraser, hunting through his drawing for round things, and Mr. Delgado paused at their table on his rounds, looked down at the oval rug, and quietly moved Daniel's paper to the top of the display case pile.
